::: {.callout-note}
## What is this exercise?

Exercises 2 through 7 each gave you a method and a dataset I chose. This one gives you **no new method and no dataset**. You bring your own project data, and you try this semester's methods on it.

Every part reuses code you've already run, with the dataset-specific details replaced by **settings** you fill in. You don't need to write new code from scratch; you need to decide what each setting should be for *your* sources, and to notice when a method doesn't fit them.

- **Parts 1–3 are for everyone:** point this file at your data, check it with Peng's EDA checklist, and make a few basic charts.
- **Part 4 is for everyone too:** turn one chart into an argument, the way Chambers does, and let a partner test it with Yau's questions.
- **Then choose at least one of Parts A–D** (Part 5 explains which kind of data each one needs):
  - **A. Distinctive words (tf-idf).** For text: which words set one group of your documents apart from the others? (E5)
  - **B. Topic modeling.** For text: which groups of words tend to appear together? (E5)
  - **C. Named entity recognition (NER).** For text: which people, places, and organizations does it name? (E6)
  - **D. Mapping.** For data with places: where are your records? (E6, E7)

Pick the part(s) that fit your question, not the ones that look easiest. Whatever you make here is a draft of your **Data Visualization & Preliminary Analysis**, due November 23.

As before, you're graded on your documented effort, not on mastery. Finish at home before Thanksgiving Break, and commit your own work.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Today in class: work in pairs

Pair up with someone whose project is **different** from yours. You each run your own file on your own laptop, side by side.

1. **Part 1 (5 minutes).** Tell your partner your answers to Q1: your question, your source, and what one row of your data is. Your partner should be able to say them back to you.
2. **Parts 2–3 (20 minutes).** Load and explore your data. When a number or a chart surprises you, show your partner, and ask whether it surprises them too.
3. **Part 4 (10 minutes).** Make your argument chart.
4. **Swap (10 minutes).** Trade laptops. Your partner answers Q7 in **your** file, and you answer it in theirs. Trade back and answer Q8.
5. **Share (5 minutes).** A few pairs show one chart to the class: its claim, and the hardest question the partner asked.

Parts 5, A–D, and 6 are for home.
:::

## Your data stays off GitHub

Your repositories are public, and project data often can't be shared: Freedom on the Move, IPUMS, copyrighted text, records about living people. This repository's `.gitignore` file tells Git to ignore every folder inside `data/`, so nothing in your folder can be committed. That only works if your data is **in a folder**: don't put files directly in `data/`. Your charts and counts in `output/exercise8/` **will** be committed, so check them before you push.
:::

### Your settings

These are the only lines you need to change for Parts 1–3. `my_folder` is your folder; `my_file` is the file inside it, as the table above shows it. Replace each other `"REPLACE-ME"` with the name of a column in your data. Leave a setting as `"REPLACE-ME"` if your data doesn't have that kind of column, and the chunks that need it will skip themselves.

```{r}
# Chunk 2
my_folder <- "data/REPLACE-ME"        # your folder: "data/" and your last name, e.g. "data/anglin"
my_file   <- "REPLACE-ME.csv"         # your file in that folder, e.g. "sc-ads.csv": a .csv or .xlsx file, a folder of .txt files, or an IPUMS .xml codebook
my_data_path <- file.path(my_folder, my_file)

category_column <- "REPLACE-ME"   # a column of categories (a type, a newspaper, a state, an occupation)
date_column     <- "REPLACE-ME"   # a column with dates or years
number_column   <- "REPLACE-ME"   # a column of numbers (an age, a price, a count)

# TRUE/FALSE switches the chunks below use to decide whether to run
has_data     <- file.exists(my_data_path) || dir.exists(my_data_path)
has_category <- has_data && category_column != "REPLACE-ME"
has_date     <- has_data && date_column != "REPLACE-ME"
has_number   <- has_data && number_column != "REPLACE-ME"

has_data
```

`has_data` should say `TRUE`. If it says `FALSE`, run `my_data_path` in the Console and check the path: it starts from this repository's folder, and capitalization matters. In RStudio's **Files** pane, you can find your file and compare its name letter by letter.

## Part 2: Read in your data

Chunk 3 looks at what kind of path you gave it and reads it the right way. A folder of text files becomes a table with one row per file: `doc_id` (the file name) and `text`. An IPUMS extract is read with `ipumsr`, as in your workspace, and its numbered codes become their labels ("Farmers (owners and tenants)" instead of `100`), except `year` and `age`, which stay numbers.

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_data
# Chunk 3
if (dir.exists(my_data_path)) {
  # a folder of .txt files: one row per file
  text_files <- list.files(my_data_path, pattern = "\\.txt$", full.names = TRUE)
  my_data <- tibble(doc_id = character(), text = character())
  for (file in text_files) {
    my_data <- bind_rows(my_data, tibble(doc_id = basename(file), text = read_file(file)))
  }
} else if (str_detect(my_data_path, "\\.xml$")) {
  # an IPUMS extract: the .xml codebook, with its .dat.gz file beside it
  library(ipumsr)
  my_data <- read_ipums_micro(my_data_path, verbose = FALSE) %>%
    rename_with(str_to_lower) %>%
    mutate(across(any_of(c("year", "age")), as.numeric)) %>%        # these stay numbers
    mutate(across(where(haven::is.labelled), haven::as_factor))      # codes -> their labels
} else if (str_detect(my_data_path, "\\.xlsx?$")) {
  my_data <- readxl::read_excel(my_data_path)
} else {
  my_data <- read_csv(my_data_path, show_col_types = FALSE)
}

my_data
```

**Q2.** Did R read your data the way you expected? Look at the column names and the first few rows. If something looks wrong (a header in the wrong row, an extra empty column, strange characters), describe it.

## Part 3: Explore your data

This part follows Peng's checklist from Exercise 4, in a shorter form.

### Check the packaging

> **Peng:** Before opening the wrapped "present," shake the box: how many rows and columns are there? And do they match what you expected? ([Peng, "Check the packaging"](https://bookdown.org/rdpeng/exdata/exploratory-data-analysis-checklist.html#check-the-packaging))

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_data
# Chunk 4
nrow(my_data)
ncol(my_data)
```

### Run `str()`, and look at the top and the bottom

> **Peng:** `str()` shows the class of every column. Make sure numbers are numbers, dates are dates, and text is text. ([Peng, "Run str()"](https://bookdown.org/rdpeng/exdata/exploratory-data-analysis-checklist.html#run-str))

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_data
# Chunk 5
str(my_data)
head(my_data)
tail(my_data)
```

### How full is each column?

Exercise 3 showed that "empty" can mean different things. This chunk counts the share of missing values (`NA`) in each column. If your data uses another way of saying "nothing here" (a dash, "unknown," `-9`), add it to `empty_values`.

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_data
# Chunk 6
empty_values <- c("", "NA", "unknown", "-9")

my_data %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), as.character)) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "value") %>%
  mutate(empty = is.na(value) | value %in% empty_values) %>%
  group_by(column) %>%
  summarize(percent_empty = round(100 * mean(empty), 1)) %>%
  arrange(desc(percent_empty))
```

### Check your "n"s

> **Peng:** Count things, and compare the counts with *landmarks*: numbers you know should be true. If you expect 1,000 people and find 20, something's wrong. ([Peng, "Check your 'n's"](https://bookdown.org/rdpeng/exdata/exploratory-data-analysis-checklist.html#check-your-ns))

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_category
# Chunk 7
my_data %>% count(.data[[category_column]], sort = TRUE)
```

(`.data[[category_column]]` means "the column whose name is stored in `category_column`." It lets the same code work for any column you name in your settings.)

**Q3.** Name one **landmark**: a number you know from outside your data (from your sources, your Close Reading, or a secondary source) that your data should match. Does it?

>

### Basic exploratory charts

Each chart below uses one of your settings, and skips itself if you left that setting as `"REPLACE-ME"`.

**Categories:** the 15 most common values in your category column.

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_category
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
# Chunk 8
my_data %>%
  count(.data[[category_column]], name = "records") %>%
  slice_max(records, n = 15, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = records, y = reorder(.data[[category_column]], records))) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey40") +
  labs(title = str_glue("Records by {category_column}"), x = "Records", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

ggsave("output/exercise8/categories.png", width = 8, height = 5, bg = "white")
```

**Time:** records per year. `str_extract()` pulls the first four-digit number out of your date column, so this works whether your dates look like `1959-10-15`, `October 15, 1959`, or `1959`.

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_date
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
# Chunk 9
by_year <- my_data %>%
  mutate(year = as.numeric(str_extract(as.character(.data[[date_column]]), "\\d{4}"))) %>%
  count(year, name = "records")

by_year %>% filter(is.na(year))   # rows whose date had no year in it

by_year %>%
  filter(!is.na(year)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = records)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey40") +
  labs(title = "Records per year", x = NULL, y = "Records") +
  theme_minimal()

ggsave("output/exercise8/records-per-year.png", width = 8, height = 4, bg = "white")
```

**Numbers:** the distribution of your number column.

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_number
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
# Chunk 10
my_numbers <- my_data %>%
  mutate(value = as.numeric(.data[[number_column]]))

summary(my_numbers$value)

ggplot(my_numbers, aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "grey40") +
  labs(title = str_glue("Distribution of {number_column}"), x = number_column, y = "Records") +
  theme_minimal()
```

If `summary()` shows many `NA's`, some values in that column aren't numbers ("about 20," "unknown"). Find them with `my_numbers %>% filter(is.na(value))`.

## Part 4: Make a chart that argues

Chambers's title is a claim, "The Gun Problem We Don't Mention," and every chart under it is there to support it. Yau shows the other side: how the way a chart is drawn can push a reader toward a conclusion the data doesn't support. In this part you do both. Make one chart whose **title states a claim** about your sources, then let a partner test whether the chart earns it.

**Q5.** Write your claim as one sentence: something about your research question that your data might show. It doesn't have to be true yet. That's what the chart is for.

>

Fill in the settings in Chunk 11:

- `claim_title` is your sentence from Q5.
- `measure` is `"count"` (how many records) or `"percent"` (each category's share of the records in that year, or in that panel). Percentages let you compare years or groups of different sizes; counts show how much there is.
- `over_time` is `TRUE` for one line per category across the years (it needs your `date_column`), or `FALSE` for bars.
- `top_n` is how many categories to show. The rest are lumped into "Other."
- `source_note` goes at the bottom of the chart. Every published chart should say where its data comes from.

Two settings are optional:

- `panel_column` splits the chart into small charts, one for each value of that column (an event, a museum, a newspaper), so you can compare them side by side.
- `search_column` and `search_words` make a category for you, if your data is mostly text: each record either mentions your words or it doesn't. Separate words with `|`, which means "or": `"insane|lunatic"`. Capitalization doesn't matter. When you set these, the chart uses them instead of your `category_column`.

Some settings to try, by workspace. They're a place to start, not the answer: your claim decides the chart.

| Workspace | Settings to try |
|---|---|
| Anglin | `passing_group` over time; or search `transcription` for your own words |
| Cole | search `clean_text` for words from your word lists, over time |
| Huneryager | search `description` for a region's names, over time (`catalog_year`) |
| Matney | `event` with `over_time <- FALSE` and `measure <- "count"`; or search `snippet` for your own words |
| Rojas | `occ1950` over time; or search `occ1950` for `"laborer"` |
| Tan | `incident_type` over time |
| Tanglertpaibul | `museum`, once you've added it, with `over_time <- FALSE` and `measure <- "count"` |

```{r}
# Chunk 11
claim_title <- "REPLACE-ME"   # your claim from Q5
measure     <- "percent"      # "count" or "percent"
over_time   <- TRUE           # TRUE: lines across the years (needs a date_column); FALSE: bars
top_n       <- 5              # how many categories to show; the rest become "Other"
source_note <- "REPLACE-ME"   # e.g. "Source: Freedom on the Move, South Carolina ads, 1732-1865"

# optional
panel_column  <- "REPLACE-ME"   # one small chart for each value of this column
search_column <- "REPLACE-ME"   # a column of text to search...
search_words  <- "REPLACE-ME"   # ...for these words, e.g. "insane|lunatic"

# switches for Chunk 12
has_search <- has_data && search_column != "REPLACE-ME" && search_words != "REPLACE-ME"
has_panel  <- has_data && panel_column != "REPLACE-ME"
use_years  <- has_date && over_time
has_claim  <- (has_category || has_search) && claim_title != "REPLACE-ME"
```

Chunk 12 draws the chart and saves it as `output/exercise8/argument-chart.png`. If you chose `over_time`, it also tells you how many records have no year, and so are **not** in the chart. Keep that number: your partner will ask about it.

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_claim
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
# Chunk 12
measure_label <- if (measure == "percent") "Percent of records" else "Records"

# 1. Give every record a category
if (has_search) {
  argument_data <- my_data %>%
    mutate(mentions = str_detect(.data[[search_column]], regex(search_words, ignore_case = TRUE)),
           category = if_else(mentions %in% TRUE,
                              str_glue("Mentions {search_words}"),
                              str_glue("Doesn't mention {search_words}")))
  category_name <- str_glue("whether {search_column} mentions {search_words}")
} else {
  argument_data <- my_data %>%
    mutate(category = as.character(.data[[category_column]]),
           category = if_else(is.na(category) | category == "", "(empty)", category),
           category = fct_lump_n(category, n = top_n, other_level = "Other"))   # the top_n, and "Other"
  category_name <- category_column
}

# 2. Give every record a panel ("all" if you didn't choose a panel_column)
if (has_panel) {
  argument_data <- argument_data %>% mutate(panel = as.character(.data[[panel_column]]))
} else {
  argument_data <- argument_data %>% mutate(panel = "all")
}

# 3. Count
if (use_years) {
  plot_data <- argument_data %>%
    mutate(year = as.numeric(str_extract(as.character(.data[[date_column]]), "\\d{4}"))) %>%
    filter(!is.na(year)) %>%
    count(panel, year, category) %>%
    group_by(panel, year) %>%
    mutate(value = if (measure == "percent") 100 * n / sum(n) else n) %>%   # share of that year's records
    ungroup()
} else {
  plot_data <- argument_data %>%
    count(panel, category) %>%
    group_by(panel) %>%
    mutate(value = if (measure == "percent") 100 * n / sum(n) else n) %>%   # share of that panel's records
    ungroup()
}
n_in_chart <- sum(plot_data$n)

# with search words and percentages, "doesn't mention" is just 100 minus "mentions", so we drop it
if (has_search && measure == "percent") {
  plot_data <- plot_data %>% filter(str_detect(category, "^Mentions"))
}

# 4. Draw
if (use_years) {
  # one line per category, across the years
  year_breaks <- pretty(plot_data$year)
  year_breaks <- year_breaks[year_breaks == round(year_breaks)]   # whole years only

  argument_chart <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = year, y = value, color = category)) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point(size = 1) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = year_breaks) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = measure_label, color = NULL)
} else {
  # one bar per category
  argument_chart <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = value, y = reorder(category, value))) +
    geom_col(fill = "grey40") +
    labs(x = measure_label, y = NULL)
}

if (has_panel) {
  argument_chart <- argument_chart + facet_wrap(vars(panel))
}

argument_chart <- argument_chart +
  labs(title    = claim_title,
       subtitle = str_glue("{measure_label}, by {category_name} (n = {format(n_in_chart, big.mark = ',')} records)"),
       caption  = if (source_note != "REPLACE-ME") source_note else NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

ggsave("output/exercise8/argument-chart.png", argument_chart, width = 9, height = 5, bg = "white")

if (use_years) {
  cat(nrow(my_data) - n_in_chart, "of your", nrow(my_data), "records have no year, so they aren't in this chart.\n")
}
argument_chart
```

## Part 5: Choose your method(s)

| Part | Method | What your data needs | From |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | Distinctive words (tf-idf) | A text column, and a column that splits documents into groups (years, decades, newspapers) | E5 |
| B | Topic modeling | A text column with **many** documents (at least 50 or so, after chunking) | E5 |
| C | Named entity recognition | A text column in English, with names in it | E6 |
| D | Mapping | A column with coordinates, addresses, or place names | E6, E7 |

Turn on the part(s) you choose by changing `FALSE` to `TRUE` below, and fill in the settings. Parts A–C share the text settings.

```{r}
# Chunk 13
do_tfidf  <- FALSE   # Part A
do_topics <- FALSE   # Part B
do_ner    <- FALSE   # Part C
do_map    <- FALSE   # Part D

# ---- text settings (Parts A, B, C) ----
text_column  <- "text"      # the column with your text ("text" if you read a folder of .txt files)
doc_column   <- "doc_id"    # a column that identifies each document
group_column <- "REPLACE-ME"   # for Part A: a column that groups documents (a year, a newspaper)
my_stopwords <- c("REPLACE-ME")   # junk words to drop: OCR fragments, words in every document

# switches for the chunks below
has_text   <- has_data && (do_tfidf || do_topics || do_ner)
run_tfidf  <- has_text && do_tfidf
run_topics <- has_text && do_topics
run_ner    <- has_text && do_ner
```

**Q9.** Which part(s) did you choose, and why do they fit your question?

>

### Prepare your text (Parts A–C)

Chunk 14 makes `docs`, one row per document, and `words`, one row per word, cleaned the way we did in E5: no stopwords, no tokens with digits, nothing shorter than three letters.

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_text
# Chunk 14
docs <- my_data %>%
  transmute(doc_id = as.character(.data[[doc_column]]),
            text   = as.character(.data[[text_column]]),
            group  = if (group_column != "REPLACE-ME") as.character(.data[[group_column]]) else "all") %>%
  filter(!is.na(text))

words <- docs %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text) %>%
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") %>%
  filter(!str_detect(word, "\\d"),
         str_length(word) >= 3,
         !word %in% my_stopwords)

nrow(docs)
words %>% count(word, sort = TRUE)
```

**Q10.** Look at the most frequent words. Which should go in `my_stopwords`? Add them and run Chunk 14 again.

>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Part A: Distinctive words (tf-idf)

In E5 you used Voyant's tf-idf to find words that set one issue of *The American City* apart from the others. `bind_tf_idf()` does the same in R: a word scores high in a group if it's frequent there and rare in the other groups. You need a `group_column` for this.

```{r}
#| eval: !expr run_tfidf
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
# Chunk A1
distinctive <- words %>%
  count(group, word) %>%
  bind_tf_idf(word, group, n) %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  slice_max(tf_idf, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup()

distinctive %>%
  mutate(word = reorder_within(word, tf_idf, group)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = tf_idf, y = word)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey40") +
  scale_y_reordered() +
  facet_wrap(~ group, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Words most distinctive of each group (tf-idf)", x = "tf-idf", y = NULL)

ggsave("output/exercise8/tfidf.png", width = 10, height = 7, bg = "white")
```

If you have many groups (say, 40 years), the chart gets crowded. Group them more broadly first, for example by decade: set `group_column` to your year column and add `mutate(group = paste0(str_sub(group, 1, 3), "0s"))` at the end of the `docs` code in Chunk 14.

**QA.** Which distinctive words are real differences in your sources, and which come from OCR errors, names, or one unusual document? Name one word you'd want to read in context.

>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Part B: Topic modeling

This is E5's topic model. Short documents (a headline, a catalog entry) are too small for a topic model, and very long ones (a whole book) are too big, so Chunk B1 cuts every document into pieces of `chunk_size` words, as we did with *The American City*.

```{r}
#| eval: !expr run_topics
# Chunk B1
library(topicmodels)   # LDA()

chunk_size     <- 1000   # words per piece
min_word_count <- 10     # drop words used fewer times than this in your whole corpus
k              <- 10     # number of topics

pieces <- words %>%
  group_by(doc_id) %>%
  mutate(piece = (row_number() - 1) %/% chunk_size) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(piece_id = paste(doc_id, piece, sep = "_"))

dtm <- pieces %>%
  add_count(word, name = "total") %>%
  filter(total >= min_word_count) %>%
  count(piece_id, word) %>%
  cast_dtm(piece_id, word, n)

dtm
```

With a small corpus, lower `min_word_count`; with a very large one, raise it so the model runs faster. Then fit the model. This can take a few minutes.

```{r}
#| eval: !expr run_topics
#| fig-height: 9
# Chunk B2
lda <- LDA(dtm, k = k, control = list(seed = 446))

top_terms <- tidy(lda, matrix = "beta") %>%
  group_by(topic) %>%
  slice_max(beta, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup()

top_terms %>%
  mutate(term = reorder_within(term, beta, topic)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = beta, y = term, fill = factor(topic))) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_y_reordered() +
  facet_wrap(~ topic, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
  labs(title = str_glue("Top 10 words in each of {k} topics"),
       x = "How typical the word is of the topic (beta)", y = NULL)

ggsave("output/exercise8/topics.png", width = 10, height = 10, bg = "white")
write_csv(top_terms, "output/exercise8/topics.csv")
```

Which documents are most made of each topic? `gamma` is the share of each piece that comes from each topic:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr run_topics
# Chunk B3
tidy(lda, matrix = "gamma") %>%
  group_by(topic) %>%
  slice_max(gamma, n = 3, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange(topic)
```

**QB.** Label three topics from their words. Then read the top piece for one of them (find it in `pieces` by its `piece_id`). Does the label hold up? Try `k = 5` and `k = 20`: which number gives topics that make the most sense for *your* sources?

>

## Part C: Named entity recognition

This is E6's model: it reads your text and tags people (`PER`), places (`LOC`), organizations (`ORG`), and other names (`MISC`). It was trained on English news from the 1990s, so expect mistakes on older or non-English text. Chunk C1 prepares the text the way the model needs it (one word per line, capitals and punctuation kept) and loads the model you downloaded in E6.

```{r}
#| eval: !expr run_ner
# Chunk C1
library(nametagger)

ner_input <- docs %>%
  mutate(sentence_id = row_number()) %>%
  unnest_tokens(term, text, token = "words", to_lower = FALSE, strip_punct = FALSE) %>%
  group_by(doc_id, sentence_id) %>%
  summarize(text = str_c(term, collapse = "\n"), .groups = "drop")

model_dir  <- tools::R_user_dir("nametagger", which = "cache")
model_path <- file.path(model_dir, "english-conll-140408.ner")

if (!file.exists(model_path)) {
  dir.create(model_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  model <- nametagger_download_model("english-conll-140408", model_dir = model_dir)
} else {
  model <- nametagger_load_model(model_path)
}
```

`tags_to_names()` is the function from E6 that glues "New" and "York" back into one name. Running the model on a large corpus takes a while, so the results are saved, and later runs read the saved file. The file goes in your `data/` folder, not `output/`, because it lists every name in your sources. **Delete `entities.csv` from your folder if you change your text and want to run the model again.**

```{r}
#| eval: !expr run_ner
# Chunk C2
tags_to_names <- function(tagged) {
  tagged %>%
    filter(entity != "O") %>%                       # keep only words inside a name
    mutate(type = str_remove(entity, "^[BI]-"),     # "B-LOC" -> "LOC"
           name_id = cumsum(str_starts(entity, "B-"))) %>%   # every B- starts a new name
    group_by(doc_id, sentence_id, name_id, type) %>%
    summarize(name = str_c(term, collapse = " "), .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(name = str_replace_all(name, "\\s+([.,;:])", "\\1")) %>%   # "St . Louis" -> "St. Louis"
    select(doc_id, type, name)
}

entities_file <- file.path(my_folder, "entities.csv")   # stays off GitHub (see Part 1)

if (!file.exists(entities_file)) {
  entities <- predict(model, ner_input) %>% tags_to_names()
  write_csv(entities, entities_file)
}

entities <- read_csv(entities_file, show_col_types = FALSE)

entities %>% count(type, sort = TRUE)

entities %>%
  count(type, name, sort = TRUE) %>%
  group_by(type) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15)
```

**QC.** Find two mistakes the model made (a place tagged as a person, a word that isn't a name). Is the model good enough for your sources, or would a list you make yourself (a gazetteer, as in E6 Part 4) work better?

>

## Part D: Mapping

You can map your records three ways, depending on what your data has. Set **one** of these:

- `lat_column` and `long_column`, if your data already has coordinates;
- `place_column`, if it has addresses or place names, which Chunk D1 will geocode;
- `use_ner_places <- TRUE`, to map the `LOC` names from Part C instead.

```{r}
# Chunk 15
lat_column     <- "REPLACE-ME"
long_column    <- "REPLACE-ME"
place_column   <- "REPLACE-ME"
use_ner_places <- FALSE

geocoder     <- "osm"   # "census" for U.S. street addresses (as in E6); "osm" for place names anywhere
place_suffix <- ""      # added to every place before geocoding, e.g. ", Singapore" or ", Muncie, IN"
popup_column <- "REPLACE-ME"   # a column to show when you click a point (a title, a name, a date)

# switches for the chunks below
run_map         <- has_data && do_map
needs_geocoding <- run_map && (place_column != "REPLACE-ME" || use_ner_places)
has_coordinates <- run_map && lat_column != "REPLACE-ME"
draw_map        <- needs_geocoding || has_coordinates
```

### Geocode (if you need to)

Chunk D1 sends each **distinct** place to the geocoder once, and saves the results in `output/exercise8/places.csv`. On later runs, only places that aren't in that file are sent, so adding records doesn't geocode everything again. OpenStreetMap allows one request per second, so a few hundred places take a few minutes.

```{r}
#| eval: !expr needs_geocoding
# Chunk D1
library(tidygeocoder)

if (use_ner_places) {
  to_map <- entities %>% filter(type == "LOC") %>% transmute(place = name, label = doc_id)
} else {
  to_map <- my_data %>%
    transmute(place = as.character(.data[[place_column]]),
              label = if (popup_column != "REPLACE-ME") as.character(.data[[popup_column]]) else place)
}

places_file <- "output/exercise8/places.csv"

if (file.exists(places_file)) {
  places <- read_csv(places_file, show_col_types = FALSE)
} else {
  places <- tibble(place = character(), lat = numeric(), long = numeric())
}

new_places <- to_map %>%
  filter(!is.na(place)) %>%
  distinct(place) %>%
  filter(!(place %in% places$place))

if (nrow(new_places) > 0) {
  message("Geocoding ", nrow(new_places), " places...")
  geocoded <- new_places %>%
    mutate(query = paste0(place, place_suffix)) %>%
    geocode(address = query, method = geocoder, lat = lat, long = long) %>%
    select(place, lat, long)
  places <- bind_rows(places, geocoded)
  write_csv(places, places_file)
}

to_map <- to_map %>%
  left_join(places, by = "place")

to_map %>% filter(is.na(lat)) %>% distinct(place)   # places the geocoder couldn't find
```

**QD1.** Look at the places the geocoder couldn't find, and five it did find. Did it put any of them in the wrong place (a modern street with the same name, the center of a city or a country)? Which of your places no longer exist?

>

### Make the maps

If your data already has coordinates, Chunk D2 uses them directly.

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_coordinates
# Chunk D2
to_map <- my_data %>%
  transmute(lat   = as.numeric(.data[[lat_column]]),
            long  = as.numeric(.data[[long_column]]),
            label = if (popup_column != "REPLACE-ME") as.character(.data[[popup_column]]) else "")
```

A static map first. The `maps` package (E6) draws country outlines; `coord_quickmap()` zooms to your points.

```{r}
#| eval: !expr draw_map
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 7
# Chunk D3
mapped <- to_map %>% filter(!is.na(lat), !is.na(long))

ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = map_data("world"), aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
               fill = "grey95", color = "grey70", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_point(data = mapped, aes(x = long, y = lat), color = "#D55E00", alpha = 0.7) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = range(mapped$long) + c(-1, 1), ylim = range(mapped$lat) + c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Your records on a map", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

ggsave("output/exercise8/map.png", width = 8, height = 7, bg = "white")
```

If your points are all in one U.S. state or city, the world outline isn't much help. E7's `tigris` layers (county roads, water, city limits) make a better base: copy Chunks 5–7 from E7 and change the county.

Then the interactive map, as in E7. Click a point to see its label.

```{r}
#| eval: !expr draw_map
# Chunk D4
library(leaflet)

my_leaflet <- leaflet(mapped) %>%
  addProviderTiles(providers$CartoDB.Positron) %>%
  addCircleMarkers(lng = ~long, lat = ~lat,
                   radius = 5, stroke = FALSE, fillOpacity = 0.8, color = "#D55E00",
                   popup = ~htmltools::htmlEscape(label))

my_leaflet

htmlwidgets::saveWidget(my_leaflet, "output/exercise8/map.html")
unlink("output/exercise8/map_files", recursive = TRUE)
```

**QD2.** What does your map show that a table of your records doesn't? What does it leave out (records with no place, places you couldn't locate, change over time)?
